FacilityDescription: Towering red and cream cliffs, the Virgin River, and famous hikes like The Narrows and Angels Landing. Utah's most visited park.
ReservationNote: No reservation to enter. Angels Landing needs a permit from a lottery on Recreation.gov.
AccessDetails: Riverside Walk is paved, about 2.2 miles round trip and mostly flat. The Pa'rus Trail is paved. Park shuttles are wheelchair accessible.
QuietTime: Weekday mornings before 8am, or December to February.
Tip: Summer highs pass 100°F. Hike early, carry at least 1 gallon (4 L) of water per person per day.
ThingsToDo: Ride the shuttle up Zion Canyon Scenic Drive
UserReviews: Priya, visiting from India
The shuttle made it easy with my parents. Riverside Walk was perfect for my dad's wheelchair.
Jake, Salt Lake City
Unreal views, but go early. Parking was full by 8am in October.

FacilityDescription: Over 2,000 natural stone arches, including Delicate Arch, the arch on Utah's license plate.
ReservationNote: Timed entry reservation needed in peak season (spring through fall). Book on Recreation.gov.
AccessDetails: Park Avenue Viewpoint, the Windows area and the lower Delicate Arch Viewpoint have accessible viewing. Most trails are uneven slickrock.
QuietTime: Before 7am or after 5pm; winter is very quiet.
Tip: Moab is the nearest town (10 minutes). Very little shade; bring sun protection.
ThingsToDo: Hike to Delicate Arch at sunset
UserReviews: Lena, Germany
Book the timed entry ahead! Sunset at Delicate Arch was the highlight of our USA trip.
Marcus, Provo
Hot and no shade in July. Spring was much better.

FacilityDescription: A giant natural amphitheater filled with orange hoodoos (rock spires). Stunning at sunrise and under snow.
AccessDetails: The Rim Trail between Sunset Point and Sunrise Point is paved and mostly flat (about 1 mile). Viewpoints along the main road are accessible.
QuietTime: Sunrise on weekdays; winter for snow and solitude.
Tip: Elevation is 8,000 to 9,000 ft (2,400 to 2,700 m). Take it slow, drink water, and pack layers even in summer.
ThingsToDo: Hike Navajo Loop and Queen's Garden
UserReviews: Aiko, Japan
Snow on the hoodoos in January was magical, and almost nobody there.
Dana, Ogden
The paved rim section worked great for our stroller.

FacilityDescription: Huge canyon views from a mesa top, carved by the Colorado and Green Rivers. Home of Mesa Arch at sunrise.
ReservationNote: No entry reservation. Backcountry camping and White Rim trips need permits.
AccessDetails: The visitor center and several overlooks, including Grand View Point overlook, are accessible. Mesa Arch trail is uneven.
QuietTime: Most days outside of sunrise at Mesa Arch.
Tip: No food or gas inside the park. Fill up in Moab, about 45 minutes away.
UserReviews: Tom, UK
Felt like the edge of the world. Much quieter than Arches.

FacilityDescription: A 100-mile wrinkle in the earth, historic Fruita orchards where you can pick fruit in season, and very dark night skies.
AccessDetails: Visitor center, Gifford Homestead and parts of the Fruita orchards are accessible. Shady picnic areas under orchard trees.
QuietTime: Most of the year; it is one of the least crowded of Utah's five national parks.
Tip: Try a fresh pie from the Gifford Homestead (seasonal). Cell service is limited.
ThingsToDo: Pick fruit in the Fruita orchards (seasonal)
UserReviews: Rosa, Mexico City
The pie! And the stars at night were the best I've ever seen.
Ben, Logan
Peaceful and uncrowded. Bring snacks; few services.

FacilityDescription: Red and white sandstone, lava tubes, and sand dunes just outside St. George. A great pick when Zion is packed.
AccessDetails: The paved Whiptail Trail runs about 3 miles along the canyon floor; good for wheelchairs, strollers and bikes.
QuietTime: Weekday mornings; winter is mild and pleasant here.
Tip: Southern Utah is warmest here. A good winter destination when the north is snowy.
ThingsToDo: Bike or roll the paved Whiptail Trail
UserReviews: Megan, St. George
Our go-to winter hike spot. The paved trail is great for little kids.

FacilityDescription: One of the most photographed overlooks in the West: a gooseneck of the Colorado River 2,000 feet below.
ReservationNote: Campsites and yurts book up; reserve ahead in spring and fall.
AccessDetails: The main overlook and visitor center are accessible, with paved sections of the rim trail.
QuietTime: Weekdays and evenings; stay for the stars (it is a Dark Sky Park).
Tip: Combine with Canyonlands: Island in the Sky; they are 15 minutes apart.
ThingsToDo: See sunset at the main overlook
Stay for a dark sky program
UserReviews: Carlos, Spain
Easy walk to one of the best views of the trip.

FacilityDescription: A valley of thousands of mushroom-shaped rock 'goblins' that kids can climb and explore freely.
AccessDetails: Overlook near the parking area gives a view of the valley. The valley floor is sand and uneven rock.
QuietTime: Weekdays outside spring break.
Tip: Remote: the nearest town with services is Hanksville, about 30 minutes away.
ThingsToDo: Climb and explore the Valley of Goblins
UserReviews: The Nguyen family, Sandy
Our kids called it a giant playground. Bring hats; no shade.

FacilityDescription: Free-roaming bison, beaches on the Great Salt Lake, and sunsets 40 minutes from Salt Lake City.
AccessDetails: Visitor center, Fielding Garr Ranch and the causeway road are accessible. Beach access is sandy.
QuietTime: Weekdays; avoid late May and June when biting gnats are heavy.
Tip: You float easily in the Great Salt Lake because it is so salty. Rinse off at the beach showers.
ThingsToDo: Float in the Great Salt Lake
UserReviews: Hannah, Australia
So close to the city and bison everywhere! Bugs were bad in early June.

FacilityDescription: The 'Caribbean of the Rockies': bright turquoise water, sandy beaches and famous raspberry shakes.
ReservationNote: Summer campsites sell out; reserve months ahead.
AccessDetails: Restrooms and some parking are accessible. Beaches are sand; check with the park about beach access options.
QuietTime: Weekdays in June or September.
Tip: The water stays cool even in July. Try a raspberry shake in Garden City.
ThingsToDo: Get a raspberry shake in Garden City
UserReviews: Sam, Layton
That water color is unreal. Book camping early.

FacilityDescription: Deep powder, steep terrain and an aerial tram to 11,000 feet, about 40 minutes from Salt Lake City.
ReservationNote: Canyon road can close for avalanche control. Check UDOT and parking rules before you go.
AccessDetails: The tram and main buildings are accessible. Adaptive ski lessons are offered at the resort through an adaptive sports partner.
QuietTime: Midweek, especially Tuesday to Thursday.
Tip: Utah snow is light and dry. Weekends and powder days bring heavy canyon traffic; go early.
ThingsToDo: Ride the aerial tram to Hidden Peak
UserReviews: Felix, Switzerland
The snow is as light as everyone says. Beat the canyon traffic by leaving early.

FacilityDescription: One of the largest ski resorts in the US, with a historic mountain town, and mountain biking and alpine coasters in summer.
AccessDetails: Base areas and Main Street are accessible. Adaptive skiing is available nearby through the National Ability Center.
QuietTime: Midweek in January (outside holidays).
Tip: Free town buses connect the resort and Main Street, so you may not need a car.
ThingsToDo: Summer: Alpine Coaster and mountain biking
UserReviews: Olivia, Brazil
Huge mountain and fun town. Expensive, but the free buses helped.

FacilityDescription: Southern Utah's ski resort, with family-friendly runs and the highest base elevation in Utah. Close to Cedar City.
AccessDetails: Lodges have accessible restrooms. Ask the resort about adaptive lessons.
QuietTime: Midweek outside holidays.
Tip: You can ski in the morning and see red rock at Cedar Breaks or Zion the same weekend.
UserReviews: Chris, Cedar City
Smaller and relaxed. Great for teaching kids to ski.

FacilityDescription: A small, artsy resort under Mount Timpanogos with uncrowded runs, a zipline and Stewart Falls hikes in summer.
AccessDetails: Main lodge and restaurants are accessible; trails are mostly natural surface.
QuietTime: Most weekdays; a calmer option than the big resorts.
Tip: About 30 minutes from Provo. Fall colors in late September are spectacular.
UserReviews: Ana, Provo
Feels like a hidden gem. The fall colors are stunning.

FacilityDescription: Park City nonprofit offering adaptive skiing, biking, horseback riding, climbing and more for people of all abilities and their families.
ReservationNote: Book lessons and programs ahead so staff and equipment can be matched to your needs.
AccessDetails: Built for accessibility. Programs support physical, cognitive, sensory and developmental disabilities, with adaptive equipment and trained instructors.
QuietTime: Ask staff about quieter session times.
Tip: A great anchor for a family trip. Pair it with Park City for the rest of the group.
UserReviews: The Ortiz family, Murray
Staff matched our son with the perfect instructor. First time he skied with his siblings.

FacilityDescription: A bright white salt plain so flat you can see the curve of the earth. Famous for land-speed racing and photos.
AccessDetails: The rest area viewpoint off I-80 has accessible parking and restrooms. The salt surface is flat but can be wet or soft.
QuietTime: Almost any time; sunrise and sunset are best for photos.
Tip: In spring the flats are often covered in water. Wash your car afterward; salt is corrosive.
UserReviews: Yuki, Japan
So strange and beautiful. Not much to do, but worth the stop on I-80.

FacilityDescription: A ranger-guided tour of three colorful caves high in American Fork Canyon.
ReservationNote: Tour tickets required and often sell out; book on Recreation.gov. Open late spring to early fall.
AccessDetails: The trail is paved but steep: about 1.5 miles each way with 1,000 ft of climbing. Not wheelchair or stroller friendly. The visitor center is accessible.
QuietTime: The first tour of a weekday.
Tip: The cave stays about 45°F (7°C) all year; bring a jacket even in July.
UserReviews: Jen, Lehi
The hike up is steep for little legs. The cave is worth it.

FacilityDescription: Zion's main campground, by the Virgin River and a short walk to the visitor center and shuttle.
ReservationNote: Reservations open months ahead on Recreation.gov and fill fast.
AccessDetails: Accessible campsites and restrooms are available. Connects to the paved Pa'rus Trail.
QuietTime: Weeknights in late fall.
Tip: Many sites have shade trees, but summer nights stay warm. Bring a fan.
UserReviews: Mark, Colorado
Best location in Zion. Book the day reservations open.

FacilityDescription: A high mountain byway past alpine lakes, wildflowers and pine forest. Cool escape from summer heat.
Cost: Recreation pass about $10 per vehicle (3 days)
ReservationNote: The upper highway closes for snow, usually from fall to late spring.
AccessDetails: Some lakeside areas have accessible paths and fishing spots. Confirm current conditions with the forest service.
QuietTime: Weekdays; side lakes away from Mirror Lake itself.
Tip: Over 10,000 ft (3,000 m). Afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer; start early.
UserReviews: Grace, Heber
Cool, green and gorgeous when the valley is 100°F.

FacilityDescription: Colorful rock chimneys and quiet trails near Bryce Canyon, named by National Geographic after the film.
AccessDetails: The short Nature Trail is mostly flat; check the surface for wheelchairs. Campground restrooms are accessible.
QuietTime: Nearly always; a calm base camp near Bryce.
Tip: Lower and warmer than Bryce, about 30 minutes away.
ThingsToDo: Use it as a quiet base for Bryce
UserReviews: Ivan, Canada
Quiet campground and colorful rocks. A great Bryce alternative.

FacilityDescription: Three massive stone bridges carved by water, and the world's first International Dark Sky Park.
AccessDetails: The 9-mile Bridge View Drive has overlooks of all three bridges; several overlooks and the visitor center are accessible.
QuietTime: Almost always quiet; remote and peaceful.
Tip: Very remote. Fill your gas tank in Blanding (about 1 hour).
UserReviews: Elena, Italy
Remote and silent. The Milky Way was incredible.
